title: AI Financing Fears Drag Tech Lower and Spill Into Credit and Rates
content:
AI anxiety shifted from equity valuations into the plumbing — the debt and capex funding the buildout — making financing risk the market's swing factor. The worry was no longer demand but leverage: whether hyperscalers and neoclouds could sustain an aggressive capex cycle, and whether it would pay off in time.

The stress built across the window. Reports that OpenAI's revenue lagged earlier signals, and Nvidia's warning that capital had turned scarce for **neoclouds**, knocked sentiment; a semiconductor rout left the Nasdaq 100 roughly **7%** below its record by late October. On the closing sessions Nvidia shed about **4.2%** and AMD near **11%**, while credit spreads widened and high yield, loans and preferreds lagged.

Crucially, the wobble handed government bonds a safe-haven bid, tightening the link between tech sentiment and rates. With leverage the vulnerability, AI **circular financing** and funding conditions stay the key risk into year-end.

title: Sticky Inflation Keeps Fed Restrictive With a December Hike in Play
content:
The higher-for-longer regime stayed the macro backbone. After September's quarter-point move — the first hike since 2023 — the Fed held the funds rate at **3.75%-4.00%** on 28 October in a split 10-2 vote, with two officials dissenting in favour of a further increase and the statement noting inflation 'remains elevated'.

The data kept the hawks in play. Headline PCE ran at **3.6%** year-on-year with core above 3%, while Q3 GDP grew a firmer-than-expected **3.4%**. The 10-year Treasury yield hovered near **5.00%**, and futures firmed towards roughly a 73% probability of a December hike despite the late-October equity wobble.

The theme mattered because elevated discount rates pressured the richest equities, housing and credit, and kept the **term premium** alive in the long end. Incoming inflation prints and the December decision remain the pivotal swing factors into year-end.

title: Middle East Supply Shock Lifts Crude to Six-Month Highs
content:
A Gulf **supply shock** ran hard through the window. Intensive tanker attacks around the Strait of Hormuz — more than 30 vessels struck — cut transit flows, Iran's Revolutionary Guards declared the strait closed on 26 October, and attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure plus the threat of US strikes after the midterms stacked further risk onto an already tight market.

Prices climbed accordingly. Brent rose around **13%** over October to a six-month high near **$118**, while weekly Hormuz export flows slipped towards **7.3m bpd** by late in the month. European gas also pushed higher, broadening the energy squeeze.

The rally mattered beyond energy: dearer crude fed directly into the hot inflation prints and hawkish rate rhetoric, reinforcing the higher-for-longer narrative. A durable recovery in Gulf flows would deflate the **risk premium**, leaving crude a key upside tail for inflation and a downside tail for risk.

title: French Fiscal Stress Widens Sovereign Spreads to Post-2011 Highs
content:
French fiscal and political stress became Europe's defining trade. Doubts over any real budget consolidation, a deficit near **5.4%** of GDP and street protests in mid-October drove the 10-year OAT-Bund spread past **150bp** early in the window and out towards **176bp** by 23 October — the widest since 2011 — with the French 10-year yield pressing near 5%.

The move spread beyond rates. The euro and Paris-listed equities softened, and analysts flagged early signs of **contagion** to other European sovereigns as elections loomed in France and Spain.

It mattered because the bloc's second-largest bond market was repricing political risk while the ECB stayed on the sidelines, having not deployed its transmission-protection tool and seen as likely to act only nearer **250-300bp**. The budget path and the ECB's reaction function remain the key watch-points into year-end.
